content: The management of neonatal withdrawal syndrome (NWS) has been inconsistent, necessitating the assessment of all infants. Infants exposed to opioids during pregnancy should remain hospitalized for at least 4–7 days after birth to monitor for withdrawal symptoms using a validated assessment tool. This tool should first be administered two hours after birth and then every four hours thereafter. Non-pharmacological interventions, such as maintaining low lighting, creating quiet environments, swaddling, and promoting skin-to-skin contact, should be implemented for all neonates exposed to alcohol and drugs during pregnancy. Despite the low quality of evidence, the recommendation to use these approaches is strong, as the benefits significantly outweigh potential harms. The values and preferences of end-users support this recommendation, and while resource consumption is acknowledged, the benefits justify the costs. A high priority is placed on identifying and preventing suffering in affected neonates. Recommendation: If required, an opioid should be used as the initial treatment for infants with neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome (NOWS). The recommendation is strong, but the quality of evidence is very low. Prolonged opioid treatment for NOWS is generally unnecessary, and shorter treatment durations are preferred. Phenobarbital may be considered as an additional therapy if there has been concurrent use of other drugs during pregnancy, such as benzodiazepines, and if opioid treatment alone does not adequately suppress symptoms. If opioids are unavailable, phenobarbital can be used as an alternative therapy. The strong recommendation to use opioids over phenobarbital, despite very low-quality evidence, is based on extensive clinical experience with opioids in managing both adult and neonatal withdrawal. Clinical experience with phenobarbital is limited. Additionally, the values and preferences of end-users favor this recommendation, and there is certainty about the balance between benefits and resource consumption. Recommendation: All infants born to women with alcohol use disorders should be assessed for signs of fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS). This recommendation is conditional due to the very low quality of evidence. Research Priorities and Gaps: There are significant gaps in knowledge regarding effective interventions for managing substance use and substance use disorders during pregnancy. Priority areas for research include psychosocial and spiritual support, programs for young children affected by maternal substance use, and better prevalence data on prescription opioid use. Further research is needed to understand the impact of substance use on maternal, fetal, neonatal, and long-term outcomes for exposed children. Questions remain about the optimal use of specific interventions during pregnancy, including screening methods, brief interventions, and detoxification protocols. Screening and Brief Interventions: Health-care workers should screen all pregnant women for alcohol and substance use as early as possible in pregnancy and at every antenatal visit. Validated screening tools are available, and health-care providers should be prepared to intervene or refer women identified as using alcohol or drugs. Brief interventions, typically lasting 5–30 minutes, should be offered to all pregnant women using alcohol or drugs. These interventions aim to assist individuals in reducing or ceasing substance use and should include feedback, advice, and follow-up. Health-care providers should receive appropriate training to deliver these interventions effectively. Implementation and Dissemination: These recommendations will be disseminated through WHO regional and country offices, collaborating centers, professional organizations, and partner agencies. Local adaptation will involve developing training materials in consultation with stakeholders and ensuring interventions are culturally appropriate and feasible within local health systems. Evaluation: The guidelines will be reviewed periodically to incorporate new evidence and developments in the field.
